title: Given an unsorted integer array, find the length of the longest run of consecutive integers. The numbers may appear in any order, and the algorithm must run in linear time.
shortTitle: Longest Consecutive Sequence — HashSet, Expand Each Potential Start

s1_definition.profdef: Finding the longest consecutive sequence in an unsorted array uses a HashSet for O(1) membership checks and then expands only from the numbers that are sequence starts, those with no predecessor present. By counting the run length forward from each true start, total work is linear because each number is visited at most twice, giving O(n) time and O(n) space without sorting.
s1_definition.analogy: The bank has a jumbled pile of account numbers and wants the longest unbroken run of consecutive numbers. The clerk dumps them all into a fast lookup set. Then for each number he checks: is the number one less than me also in the set? If yes, I am in the middle of a run, skip me. If no, I am the start of a run, so I count upward, me, me plus one, me plus two, until the chain breaks.
s1_definition.oneliner: Put everything in a set, start counting only from numbers whose predecessor is absent, and expand forward.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Finding the longest consecutive sequence in an unsorted array uses a HashSet for O(1) membership checks and then expands only from the numbers that are sequence starts, those with no predecessor present. By counting the run length forward from each true start, total work is linear because each number is visited at most twice, giving O(n) time and O(n) space without sorting.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The bank has a jumbled pile of account numbers and wants the longest unbroken run of consecutive numbers. The clerk dumps them all into a fast lookup set. Then for each number he checks: is the number one less than me also in the set? If yes, I am in the middle of a run, skip me. If no, I am the start of a run, so I count upward, me, me plus one, me plus two, until the chain breaks.

**One line to remember:** Put everything in a set, start counting only from numbers whose predecessor is absent, and expand forward.

sections.s2_technical:
The naive approach sorts the array in O(n log n) then scans for runs. The linear approach avoids sorting by using a HashSet for constant-time lookups and being clever about where it starts counting.

First we add all numbers to a HashSet, which also deduplicates. For example, `Set<Integer> set = new HashSet<>(); for (int x : nums) set.add(x);`.

Then the key insight: we only begin counting a run at a number that is a true start, meaning the number minus one is not in the set. For example, `if (!set.contains(x - 1))`. If x minus one is present, x is in the middle of some run and counting from it would be redundant work.

From each true start, we expand forward: `int current = x, length = 1; while (set.contains(current + 1)) { current++; length++; }` and track the maximum length seen.

The linearity argument is subtle and important: although there is a loop inside a loop, the inner while loop only runs for true starts, and across all true starts it visits each number exactly once, so the total inner-loop work is O(n). Combined with the O(n) outer scan, the whole thing is O(n). Each number is touched at most twice, once in the outer loop and once in an inner expansion.

A senior-level nuance is exactly this amortized analysis; a naive reading looks quadratic, but the start-only guard guarantees each element is expanded through just once. Being able to explain why it is linear, not just claim it, is what interviewers probe.

Another nuance is that the HashSet deduplicates automatically, so repeated values do not inflate the count, and the expansion naturally handles gaps because the while loop stops at the first missing successor.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — National Bank of India issues cheque serial numbers, and due to batch processing they arrive unsorted. The fraud team wants the longest run of consecutive serial numbers present in a batch, because an unusually long consecutive run can indicate a bulk-issued block worth reviewing. This is exactly the longest-consecutive-sequence problem.

Problem 2 — Sorting the serials to find runs would be n-log-n and too slow on very large batches processed in real time, so we use the HashSet linear method.

Problem 3 — Serials can contain duplicates from reprocessing, which the HashSet deduplicates automatically, and gaps between blocks are handled because expansion stops at the first missing successor.

In the code: a `SequenceFinder` has a `longestConsecutive` method using the HashSet start-expand technique. A `ConsecutiveDemo` main finds the longest run in a jumbled serial array.

sections.s5_journey:
Input: serials 100, 4, 200, 1, 3, 2, 101, 102, 103.

Step 1: Add all to the set, which holds 1, 2, 3, 4, 100, 101, 102, 103, 200.

Step 2: Iterate the set. For 1, is 0 in the set? No, so 1 is a true start. Expand: 2 present, 3 present, 4 present, 5 absent. Run length is 4.

Step 3: For 2, is 1 in the set? Yes, so 2 is mid-run, skip. Same for 3 and 4, skipped.

Step 4: For 100, is 99 in the set? No, true start. Expand: 101, 102, 103 present, 104 absent. Run length is 4.

Step 5: For 101, 102, 103, predecessor present, skipped.

Step 6: For 200, is 199 present? No, true start. Expand: 201 absent. Run length is 1.

The maximum run length is 4, from either the block 1 to 4 or the block 100 to 103.

Final output:

```
2026-10-26 23:25:00 [INFO] Finding the longest run of consecutive cheque serials
2026-10-26 23:25:00 [INFO] Longest consecutive run length -> 4
```
sections.s5b_flow:
```
  Input: [100 4 200 1 3 2 101 102 103]
    │
    ▼ load into HashSet {1 2 3 4 100 101 102 103 200}
    │
    ▼ expand only from true starts (x-1 absent)
  start 1   → 1,2,3,4      len 4
  start 100 → 100,101,102,103 len 4
  start 200 → 200          len 1
  (2,3,4,101,102,103 skipped: predecessor present)
    │
    ▼
  Output: longest run = 4
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Finding the longest run of consecutive integers in an unsorted array in linear time comes down to two ideas: a HashSet for constant-time membership checks, and the discipline of only beginning to count a run from a number that is a genuine start. A number is a genuine start when the value one less than it is not in the set, because if its predecessor were present it would just be somewhere in the middle of a longer run and counting from it would repeat work. From each true start I walk forward, checking for the successor one at a time until the chain breaks, and I track the longest run.

The part that trips people up is the time complexity. It looks like a loop inside a loop, which suggests quadratic, but the start-only guard guarantees that the inner expansion runs only once per run and visits each number exactly once across the whole execution. So every element is touched at most twice, once by the outer scan and once by a single inner expansion, which makes the total linear. Being able to explain that amortized argument, rather than just asserting it is linear, is what demonstrates I actually understand the algorithm.

In my banking project at National Bank of India, cheque serial numbers arrive unsorted from batch processing, and the fraud team wants the longest run of consecutive serials in a batch, because a very long consecutive block can signal a bulk-issued set worth reviewing. This method finds it without sorting, which matters because sorting a huge real-time batch would add an n-log-n cost we want to avoid.

Two practical benefits I mention are that the HashSet deduplicates automatically, so reprocessed duplicate serials do not inflate the run length, and that gaps between serial blocks are handled naturally because the forward expansion stops at the first missing successor. The whole thing is a clean example of trading a sort for a hash-set-backed linear scan.
